---
title: "Methodology"
---

How every number on this site is made, in enough detail to reproduce one. The code is in the
[repository](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence); each step below names
the file that does it.

## The pipeline

Every scheduled run goes through the same six steps.

1. **Collect.** One small script per source fetches the latest file or API response and
   saves it untouched, with the retrieval time, the URL and a checksum.
2. **Validate.** A schema check confirms the columns, types and value ranges look right. If
   they do not, the run stops and opens a GitHub Issue, and the site keeps showing the last
   good data.
3. **Transform.** Raw files become tidy tables: one row per entity per date, standard units,
   standard names.
4. **Model.** Baselines, regressions and residuals are computed from the tidy tables.
5. **Export.** Each page gets a small JSON file under `data/v1/` holding only what it shows,
   with its own label: source, retrieval date, frequency, typical lag and known limitations.
6. **Build and deploy.** Quarto renders the pages from those files and the workflow
   publishes them.

Raw responses are never edited and never published. Fixes happen in transform code, so any
number can be rebuilt from its source. The files under
[`data/v1/`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/tree/main/site/data/v1)
are a contract: pages read only from them, by fixed paths and fixed column names.

### Silent failures and the heartbeat

A run that fails loudly opens an Issue. A **silent failure** is a day the site falls behind
with nothing to say so: the schedule did not fire, or a run went green without collecting
anything new. A heartbeat workflow looks twice a day, at 03:05 and 21:05 UTC, and opens one
Issue when the daily run has not succeeded on the main branch in 48 hours, the weekly run in
nine days, or any published file is out of date: a source retrieved longer ago than its
allowance (two days for daily sources, nine for weekly ones), a file not regenerated within two
days, or a key table empty. It closes the Issue when every check passes. GitHub starts
scheduled runs hours late on free accounts, so the 48-hour window is wide on purpose. The
monthly brief lists the days with no successful run. GitHub can also drop a scheduled start altogether, so
the daily workflow has a second slot at 19:47 UTC that does nothing if a run already succeeded
that day.

## Trade and Supply Chain

US general imports at customs value, by country of origin and two-digit Harmonized System
chapter, monthly from 2013, from the Census Bureau's international trade API. Seven partners
are kept: China and the six Southeast Asian economies, plus the total for all countries.

**Share shift.** A partner's share of a chapter is its imports over twelve months divided by
imports from all countries over the same twelve months. Twelve months removes the seasons. The
shift is the latest share minus the share in calendar 2017, the last year before the first US
Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods (July 2018). A chapter a partner did not ship in a month
counts as zero. The table of China against Southeast Asia lists chapters of at least
\$5 billion a year. These are observations: a share that rose beside one that fell is not
evidence the same goods moved.

**Matching Census.** For every partner and month, the chapters are summed and compared with
the all-commodity total, asked for in a separate call. If any differs by more than 1%, the run
stops and nothing is stored. The check is published on the trade page.

**Lead-time test.** The claim: US imports from an economy say something about that economy's
total exports before its own figure is out. For each economy the target is the year-on-year
growth of its goods exports (IMF). The baseline is the same growth one month earlier. The model
is a straight line on that lagged growth and on the year-on-year growth of US imports from the
economy in the same month. It is fitted on months to December 2022 and scored once on every
later month. The claim is shown for an economy only if the model's average error beats the
baseline's by more than twice the standard error of the gain; otherwise it is dropped. Both
series are today's revised figures, so the test is kinder than real time.

The base year, the size threshold, the 1% tolerance and every rule of the lead-time test were
written in
[`pdi/trade/config.py`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/pdi/trade/config.py)
on 15 November 2026, before any trade figure was collected.

## Federal Procurement

Federal contract transactions from USAspending.gov, which republishes the Federal Procurement
Data System. The first slice is computer hardware bought by every agency, from October 2016.

**The slice.** Contracts and orders (not grants, loans or umbrella agreements) whose Product
and Service Code is a hardware code: computers and servers, storage, data centre equipment,
and desktops, laptops and printers. Software, supplies, networks, radios and mobile devices
are left out. The government rewrote its code list on 1 October 2020, so figures before and
after that month are not on the same footing, and the newer codes cover hardware together with
software sold under a perpetual licence. The full list of codes is in the config file.

**Three kinds of money.** Promised (obligation), the ceiling (the value if every option is
used) and paid (outlay) are kept in three columns from the download to the page and are never
added together. Monthly value, concentration and competition use money promised. Paid is
compared with promised only over the awards that report a paid figure, and the page shows how
many do.

**What is stored.** USAspending builds a file of transactions on request, one per fiscal year.
The collector asks only for sixteen columns, none about a person or an address, and stores
sums: by month, agency and code; by supplier and fiscal year; by how the award was competed;
and by the year an award began. The transactions are not committed. A name is stored only for
the 25 largest suppliers of a fiscal year; every other supplier is an id.

**Supplier names.** A supplier is the parent company the source names, else the company on
the contract. Groups whose names are identical after removing case, punctuation and legal
endings (Inc, LLC, Corp and so on) are merged. The page reports how many names, registrations
and groups there were at each step.

**Metrics.** *Concentration*: each supplier's share of net obligations in a fiscal year, among
suppliers above zero; the share of the largest 4 and 10; and the Herfindahl-Hirschman index.
*New entrant*: a supplier above zero in a year with no action in the slice in the four fiscal
years before. *Single-bidder share*: of dollars newly obligated on awards marked as competed
and with a number of offers recorded, the share on awards that drew one offer. All are
observations.

**Matching USAspending.** For every month, the downloaded transactions are summed and compared
with the monthly figure from USAspending's own search for the same filters. The criterion is
that every month is within 1%. The figures are shown either way with the verdict beside them.
When months miss, the collector lists the transactions behind the search figure for the six
worst months and counts the ones that appear twice under the same internal id; that diagnosis
is shown next to the verdict and does not change it.

**Provisional months.** Department of Defense records are published 90 days late. Months and
fiscal years that ended fewer than 90 days before retrieval are marked provisional and are
left out of the headline sentences.

Every code, threshold and rule was written in
[`pdi/procurement/config.py`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/pdi/procurement/config.py)
on 15 November 2026, before the module's figures were computed. The file says what had been
seen at that point.

## Energy Demand

One measure: monthly electricity demand, in terawatt-hours, from
[Ember's monthly electricity data](https://ember-energy.org/data/monthly-electricity-data)
(CC BY 4.0). Ember applies one definition to every country: electricity generated plus net
imports. It covers the United States, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and
Vietnam; it has no monthly demand for Indonesia.

1. **Per day.** Each month's demand is divided by the days in the month, so a 28-day February
   does not read as a fall.
2. **Change on a year earlier.** Demand per day against the same month a year before, and the
   last twelve months against the twelve before.
3. **Index.** Demand per day with the 2019 average as 100, the first full year all six
   economies have, so that a small and a large grid fit on one chart.
4. **Unusual month.** The Macro Monitor's rule, unchanged: the monthly move against the median
   move of the same calendar month in up to ten earlier years, flagged at 2.5 spreads. It needs
   five earlier years of that month.

The collector stops the run when a covered country is missing, a value is outside 0.5 to 1,000
TWh, or demand no longer equals generation plus net imports in the file. Everything on the page
is an observation. Southeast Asian histories start between 2009 and 2019, so "unusual" there
rests on five to seven earlier years. Oil demand was considered and left out: JODI's terms
reserve all rights and grant no reuse.

## Monthly brief

On the first daily run of each month, code writes a short brief of what changed in the month
before: new readings and revisions, flags and how earlier flags turned out, price moves of 5%
or more, the latest verdicts of the out-of-sample tests, and the days the pipeline did not run.
Nothing in it is written by hand, and each line carries its finding label. Briefs are under
[Monthly brief](briefs/index.qmd).

## Rules the pipeline enforces

1. **Baseline before model.** Every model page shows a naive comparison. A model that does
   not beat it is published as "no signal found", which is a result.
2. **Split by time, never at random.** Train on the past, test on what came after.
3. **Write the test before looking at outcomes.** Split dates and thresholds are committed in
   code before the first result is seen.
4. **Count the attempts.** Everything tried is listed in the [failures log](failures.qmd).
5. **Respect small samples.** Prefer the simpler model when the gap is within noise.
6. **Never mix incomparable measurements.** Different benchmark versions, listing and
   transaction prices, base and peak scores: separate columns, never averaged together.
7. **Label every number.** The label comes from the metadata file, so it cannot be forgotten.
8. **Say what kind of finding it is.** Every finding carries one of the three labels below.

## Finding labels

Each finding on this site is tagged with what kind of claim it is. The tag is set in code from
the test result, never typed by hand on a page
([`pdi/common/findings.py`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/pdi/common/findings.py)).

| Label | What it means | What it does not mean |
|---|---|---|
| [Observation]{.finding .finding-observation} | A measured value, or simple arithmetic on measured values, such as score divided by price. No model is involved. | It says nothing about why, or about what comes next. |
| [Explanation]{.finding .finding-explanation} | A fitted model describes a relationship, such as how score rises with core count, or what is left over after it. | The model has not shown it predicts data it never saw better than the naive baseline, so it is a description, not a forecast. |
| [Prediction]{.finding .finding-prediction} | A model's output, published only because that model beat the naive baseline on data it never saw, by more than the noise level fixed before the test. | It is not certain. The page shows the size of its typical error. |

A finding moves up to **prediction** only by passing its module's out-of-sample test. If a
later run fails the test, the label drops back on that run, automatically.

## Tech Value

### Benchmarks

Two open benchmark sources are used for two different jobs, and their scores are never
combined.

- **SPEC CPU 2017** results are submitted by hardware vendors under a published run rule, and
  each one discloses the full tested configuration. That makes them the ground truth for the
  specification model. They are dominated by servers. One suite and one metric are used:
  **SPECrate 2017 Integer, base**.
- **Blender Open Data** is crowd-submitted and covers consumer CPUs and graphics cards. It is
  used for the value ranking. A launch counts only if it used a single device and finished all
  three standard scenes; its score is the sum of samples per minute over those scenes. Scores
  are grouped by device, compute backend and Blender version, a group needs at least five
  runs, and the ranking uses a single Blender version.

### Prices

Prices are collected once a day by a crawler that searches each retailer for each benchmarked
model. A retailer is used only if its robots.txt allows the page and it answers a client that
says what it is; the crawler waits between requests and does nothing to get past a bot wall.
Most large US retailers block automated clients, so coverage is a small part of the market
and is listed on the [sources page](sources.qmd). The price of a model is its cheapest new
listing that is in stock on the collection date. Refurbished and open-box listings and
accessories are left out. These are listing prices, not what anyone paid. Daily prices cannot be
backfilled, so the history starts on the day the collector was switched on.

Once a week, Amazon US and Best Buy listings are added from a data provider, Bright Data.
Amazon's conditions of use exclude collecting and reusing its prices, and Best Buy's rows are
treated the same way, so the raw rows from both are kept out of the public repository. Only the lowest price per model, its history and the fair price
built from it are published.

Amazon's data has no field for a listing's condition, so only new stock that can be vouched
for is counted: a listing must be sold by Amazon.com itself or by the part's own brand. Every
marketplace seller is left out, because a used part offered under a new-looking listing cannot
be told apart from a new one. Listings filed under "Amazon Renewed" or sold by Amazon Resale
are dropped as well. The cost is coverage: older parts that Amazon no longer stocks have no
Amazon price.

Best Buy's search is loose and returns other models and whole PCs beside the part asked for.
A Best Buy listing counts only if Best Buy files it as a bare processor or graphics card,
Best Buy is the seller, the title does not mark it refurbished, open-box or pre-owned, and
its name parses to exactly the model searched for.

Retail listings and benchmark devices are matched by a model key parsed from their names
(`pdi/tech_value/names.py`). A name that is not recognised is left unmatched and counted on the
coverage table. Nothing is matched by guesswork.

### The model

The target is the log of the SPEC score of one published result.

- **Naive baseline:** score is proportional to cores times clock speed. One constant is fitted.
- **Plain regression:** ordinary least squares on log cores, log clock speed, log chips,
  multithreading, log cache per core (L2 and L3), vendor, and years since 2017 at first
  availability.
- **AutoGluon Tabular:** trains boosted trees, random forests and ensembles of them on the same
  information, on a weekly schedule with a fixed time limit on CPU.

Processors are assigned to a period by the first hardware-availability date they appear with,
so one processor is never on both sides of a split. Models are fitted on the training period.
The validation period ranks them and makes the pick. The holdout, which is the newest
generation, is scored once for the pick and for the two reference models.

The pick has to beat the baseline on the holdout by more than the fold-to-fold spread: the
standard deviation, across expanding time-ordered folds, of the baseline error minus the plain
model error. Otherwise the baseline is published. The current result, the leaderboard and the
split dates are on the [model page](tech-value/model.qmd).

### Residuals

The ranking of over- and under-performers uses out-of-fold predictions from the plain
regression: each processor is predicted by a model fitted without any of its results. A
processor's residual is the median over its results, and it needs at least three.

A residual is not a quality score. SPEC results for the same processor differ with memory,
compiler and operating system, and vendors choose which configurations to submit. The tested
configuration is shown beside each residual so that it can be checked first.

### Reproduce one number by hand

This is for someone who has not seen the code. It needs Python with pandas and nothing from
this repository except one standalone script, and it rebuilds the US consumer prices row of the
flag table.

1. Download
   [`scripts/reproduce_headline.py`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/scripts/reproduce_headline.py)
   and run `pip install pandas`.
2. Run `python reproduce_headline.py`. It downloads CPIAUCSL (consumer prices, all items,
   seasonally adjusted) from FRED's public CSV. To work offline, save that CSV from the
   [FRED page](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL) and pass its path.
3. The script applies the four steps above to the latest month: the move, the median of the
   previous 120 calendar months, the spread (1.4826 times the median absolute deviation) and
   the number of spreads. A month FRED left blank stays a gap; October 2025 has none because of
   the US government shutdown, so there is no October or November 2025 move.
4. Compare its last line with the `US.cpi` row of
   [`data/v1/macro/series.json`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/site/data/v1/macro/series.json)
   (columns `move`, `expected_move` and `z`) for the same day. For October 2026, collected on
   15 November 2026, both give a move of 0.350, a usual move of 0.257 and 0.45 spreads.

A test (`tests/test_reproduce.py`) checks on every change that the script and the pipeline
agree. Whether a stranger can follow the steps without help is checked only by a stranger
doing it; until one has, that part of the Harden phase stays open.

### Rebuilding with the pipeline

```bash
uv sync --extra site
uv run python -m pdi.tech_value.spec      # collect and tidy SPEC results
uv run python -m pdi.tech_value.export    # fit the plain model and write data/v1/
```

The holdout error of the plain regression in `site/data/v1/tech-value/holdout.json` should
match the model page for the same retrieval date.

## Macro Monitor

### Series

About 25 monthly US series come from FRED, and only those first published by a US federal
agency. The six Southeast Asian economies are covered by two international tables that put each
measure on one definition for every country, which is what makes a comparison between
neighbours fair:

* the **BIS** tables of policy rates, consumer prices, exchange rates and real effective
  exchange rates;
* the **IMF** tables of goods exports and imports in US dollars and official reserves excluding
  gold, for all six, and consumer prices for Vietnam, which the BIS does not publish. IMF series
  start in January 2011, because Singapore's trade figures change basis in 2004 and again in
  2010 and a single start date keeps the six comparable.

Malaysia has five more series from its statistics office. The full list is on
the [series page](macro/series.qmd) and in
[`pdi/macro/config.py`](https://github.com/liumOazed/public-data-intelligence/blob/main/pdi/macro/config.py).

Coverage is uneven and the page says so: Vietnam and Singapore have no policy rate in these
tables, industrial production is not included because the IMF's table for these six ends in
2025 or earlier, and national sources other than Malaysia's are not wired in. IMF data may be
republished with attribution; commercial reuse needs the IMF's permission.

### How a flag is made

For every series and month:

1. **Move.** For levels (prices, jobs, output, exchange rates), 100 times the change in the
   log of the value, which is close to the percent change. For rates, the change in the rate.
2. **Usual move.** The median move over the previous ten years. For series that are not
   seasonally adjusted, the median move in the same calendar month over those years.
3. **Surprise.** The move minus the usual move.
4. **Spreads.** The surprise divided by the series' usual spread: 1.4826 times the median
   absolute deviation of its surprises over the same ten years, a measure that large past
   shocks do not inflate. For series that rarely move at all, such as policy rates, the
   standard deviation is used.

A reading is flagged at 2.5 spreads or more. Only data before the month being scored is used,
so a flag in the backtest is the flag the rule would have raised at the time, with one
caveat: the values are today's revised figures, not the ones first published.

**Against neighbours.** For each BIS measure and each IMF trade and reserves measure, a country's spreads minus the median spreads of
the other Southeast Asian economies in the same month, scored the same way against that gap's
own ten years. It needs at least three other countries reporting that month.

The thresholds, the ten-year window and the rule for whether a flag held were written in the
config file on 15 November 2026, before any flag was computed. Every flag is an observation:
it is arithmetic on published values with no fitted model.

### Forecast test

A flag says a move was large. Whether next month's move can be forecast is a separate
question, tested on the [forecast page](macro/model.qmd) with AutoGluon TimeSeries against
four rules of thumb. Forecasts appear on the site, labelled as predictions, only on runs
where the picked model beat the best rule of thumb on months it never saw.

### Revisions

Macro figures are revised. From its first run the pipeline keeps every value as it was first
seen, with the date, in `data/store/macro/vintages.parquet`, and only ever appends to it.
Once that has a year of history the backtest can be rerun on what was known at the time.

### Rebuilding with the pipeline

```bash
uv sync --extra site
uv run python -m pdi.macro.collect     # needs no key; FRED_API_KEY is used when set
uv run python -m pdi.macro.export      # computes flags and writes data/v1/macro/
```
